utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we have the witness today, I would like to say that we are very sorry that Judge Clark won't be able to be with us for today and tomorrow. In accordance with the Rule 15 bis, the remaining Judges decided to sit for another two days. That's so decided. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before -- I'm sorry, before the usher comes in, Your Honour, we've just learned literally five minutes ago that the order for the witnesses this week has again changed dramatically. Apparently, unbeknownst to us until just a few minutes ago, the two witnesses, the two next witnesses who have been here have been sent home, leaving the next two witnesses after Mr. -- I'm not sure -- the current witness, to be two other witnesses who we had not intended -- expected to be called until sometime later. This is again apparently continues to be trial by ambush, Your Honour, and we are not prepared to proceed with either of those two witnesses on cross-examination, either of the two, and again I won't use their names out of an abundance of caution. I don't know why someone on my staff cannot have been communicated with at least on Friday. We did not receive anything. Apparently, a fax came into my office late on Friday afternoon. It was sent to me. Counsel obviously knew that I was not in my office on Friday. So it was not known to any member of the Prosecution staff until literally about seven minutes ago. We are not prepared to proceed with these witnesses. We will be denied a fair opportunity for cross-examination if cross-examination has to go forward on this basis. We simply cannot conduct business this way, Mr. President. We change every day, the order changes all the time. No one tells us. Apparently, some people knew that this had happened. We didn't. We cannot prepare to meet these witnesses, important witnesses for the Chamber, and to assist the Chamber with cross-examination without having knowledge and the ability to prepare for the witnesses ahead of time. We have no knowledge of this and it's a complete surprise to us. We object to doing business in this way. We are not prepared to cross-examine either of these men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really do not understand it. The Prosecutor knows very well what submissions he tendered in and he knew very well that two witnesses, for which they pleaded with the Court to be given time for, that it might very well happen that two Defence witnesses could come late, and this is what happened. At 5.00, we received a message that they would be summoned at a later point in time. Now, if the Prosecutor seems to be discontent with this, then obviously it applies also to the Defence. The Defence must be ready at any point in time and must be willing to call the witnesses. It is not due to the Defence, its intentions or whatever. We have not been changing the lists of witnesses. We had to change the order of one witness because of his illness. All the others were called in the order in which they were announced. However, the Prosecution requested time and again to change the order of their witnesses. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, can you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution requested that two witnesses be postponed and the Court accepted their motion, and in fact, the learned friend knew who the following two witnesses would be for more than two weeks, in fact, for more -- a lot more than two weeks. You asked the two witnesses to be postponed. Now everybody knew which would be the next two witnesses, but if the learned friend is not ready, then the Defence has nothing against postponing these two witnesses. Your Honours, whether this is an opportunity -- a situation where they need time to prepare, this is fine with us. We have nothing against it. We will be working for three working days this week anyhow and we -- as far as the Defence is concerned, we have no objections for the examination to be postponed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, last Friday morning, we held a hearing upon the motion filed by the Prosecution on the testimony of the two witnesses, namely, the two witnesses is the fourth and the sixth witnesses on the list filed by the Defence counsel on April 3rd, 2002. On that afternoon, after deliberations among the Judges, we decided to postpone the testimony of these two witnesses until later stage. The written decision will be rendered today, and this week, we only have four working days, that is from Monday to Thursday, and according to the list filed by the Defence counsel on April 3rd, 2002, there are six witnesses on that list. We believe that the Prosecution has been informed about these six witnesses already so we don't think there is a surprise attack on both parties. We will continue to hear the witnesses on this list, except the two witnesses who have been back. It's so decided. Mr. Krsnik, could you please inform us about the translation issues? Because it's a big issue and all the documents have been piled up. Have you got all those translations for the pertinent witness for today and for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the witness today, we basically have all documents translated, and I'm pleased to tell you. As far as tomorrow goes, I'm not quite sure that all translations are ready, but in the course of this afternoon we will verify the situation, but for the next witness we basically have all documents translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear the interpreter very well, Your Honour, but I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, shall we try it again? Can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, on Friday when we left off, we were discussing your political views and in light of that issue, I would like you to be shown Exhibit IAC-2 again, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours, but I cannot hear the interpreter once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe someone in the booth could help us to straighten it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is very well now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, witness, this is document IAC-2 which was shown to you by the Defence in your examination-in-chief. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can remember this document from here, from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, you testified that you felt that this was not an authentic document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, I don't know if you had a chance of reading this document but this document talks about a meeting that was held in Grude on the 12th of November, 1991, and my question is, do you recall that that meeting ever took place?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall it. We had many meetings and as far as this one is concerned, I cannot define it either in terms of place or time, particularly as far as this content is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. The document is dated 12 November, so this was six days before the -- before the founding of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the meeting was allegedly held in Grude, which is the municipality where you were the President of the Grude municipal assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the President of the municipal assembly of Grude, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the document, it says that it was a joint meeting of the Herzegovina regional committee -- excuse me, a joint meeting of the Herzegovina regional community and the Travnik regional community. Now, let's assume that such a meeting took place. Would you have been invited in your function as a president of the Grude municipal assembly for such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the host, at any rate, whenever meetings were held in my municipality. And as a host, I took care of technical matters just as the ushers here are taking care of the witnesses, their being brought into the courtroom, et cetera. So I was requested to provide for the premises and all the other technical details for the meetings to be held. But I could not attend all the meetings and as far as this one is concerned, I therefore cannot place it in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you testified, you said that you would have been the host. Would that also -- would that also explain that you, on this document, are mentioned as the clerk? Which is on the last page, underneath the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not be the clerk or the recording clerk under any conditions. My position of the President of the municipal assembly required me to take care of other businesses. I had about 100 employees and some of them were lawyers, were clerks, who could be much more competent to keep the minutes of this meeting, much more than I personally could do it since I'm a professor of literature and history of arts by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, I would thus be at the level -- put down to the level of the recording clerk but that was usually not the type of job that I would perform. I was the President of the municipal assembly of Grude, and I would usually not do this type of record keeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, but as a host, as the President of the Grude, you would be responsible for the work of the clerks, you would be the person the clerks would be working for; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not correct. Being a lawyer yourself, you'll probably know very well that whenever the agenda is drafted for a meeting, at the same time the recording clerk is also appointed. Therefore, as a host, I cannot be held responsible in any way whatsoever for the meetings -- for the minutes of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, once again, so you testified that you can't recall that there was a meeting on the 12th of November, or are you testifying that there may have been a meeting but that you were not present? Could we be clear on that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present -- if I was not involved in POWs exchange on that day, I usually was the host of the meetings that were held in my office in the conference hall of the municipal assembly at Grude, but I cannot recall whether, on the 12th of November, 1991, this meeting was held there. I can assure you however, that I did not attend this meeting and I was not the recording clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's have a closer look at the document. First all, let's look at the persons who -- well, their signatures do not appear but the document underneath next to the date, it says -- it says Mate Boban and Dario Kordic. Do you know these two names?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What is your relationship with Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had a fair relationship, in which Mr. Boban, in terms of the hierarchy of the authorities, was my superior and I always respected this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you share the political views of Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I shared political views with Mr. Boban, you will know that political views are such a subtle matter that one changes them over a longer period of time in himself, let alone when comparing them to some other person's. Obviously, a man is a human being, allowed to think, to formulate, all sorts of attitude towards life including political opinions and views.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were you a personal friend of Mr. Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not know Mr. Boban before 1990, and the period in which we met from 1990 onward was not really the ideal period for friendships to be built and develop. Friendships are made in childhood, in the course of your studies, in the first years of your professional life. But I can assure you that we had a correct and fair relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's look at the content of the document. I'd like you to look at -- well, it reads, "Conclusions," and then there are three conclusions. And let's look at the first conclusion. And I'd like you to move somewhere to the middle of that paragraph, starting with the date 12 November, 1991. And for the English translation, it's on the top of page number 3. Let me read out to you what's written here: "On this occasion, 12 November, 1991, these two regional communities have unanimously decided that the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina must finally embrace a determined and active policy which will realise our eternal dream, a common Croatian state." My question is, Mr. Maric, was this also your political view in 1991, that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina should embrace a determined and active policy to realise the eternal dream, a common Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal political views in 1991 would be as follows. Yugoslavia as a state no longer can exist. Within the framework of the process of new, emerging states, the Croatian people in Croatia will be able to live within their own state and the constitutive people of Croats will also be able to establish their independent state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These were the views prior to the war. When the war broke out, when all possibilities, in fact, were open, there have been different speculations entertained, but when the Badinter Commission decided that the borders of the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot be changed, I, being a politically mature person, knew that this is what was defined for the future by the European Union and by the international community at large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, please speak slowly because whatever you said had to be translated into the other two languages. The interpreters, especially the French interpretation, is far behind you. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, let's read out something else from this document, and I will just continue where I stopped. Paragraph 1. The document continues to read, "In order that historical goal may soon also be our reality, these two regional communities asked that legal and political documents be prepared and published. Proclaiming a Croatian Banovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the holding of a referendum on joining the Republic of Croatia as the first step on the road to the final solution of the Croatian question and the creation of -- " and then the text becomes rather illegible. Now, witness, isn't it true that the official creation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna six days after this alleged meeting was that not the first step on the road to the final solution of the Croatian question?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The establishment of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna on the 18th of November, in all its statutes and provisions, emphasised that this document is incoherent, is in contradiction with the document here, the thing that you consider to be the document. The document on the establishment of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna stipulates very clearly that it will remain within the framework of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This can be seen both in the preamble, where it says at the beginning, "Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Herzegovina regional community," and this can also be seen and is reflected in the contents of the document as well. Therefore, it would not be logical to, on the basis of this so-called document, draw any comparison with the act of the -- through which the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna was officially proclaimed because these two documents exclude one another, that is your interpretation is being excluded, your interpretation of the document in my hand, when compared to the official document that nobody has contested, as far as its authenticity goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let me make one more quote from this document, and I'd like to have your comment on that. This is on paragraph 2, and it's the last sentence. And this sentence is underlined and it says the following: "Our people will not accept under any conditions any other solution except within the borders of a free Croatia." And the borders of a free Croatia are underlined again. Now, Mr. Maric, was that not indeed your view as well that the Croats would not agree to any other solution except within the borders of a free Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true. It is precisely this explicit text shows, well, because it would have been a complete turnaround six days before the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. document on the establishment of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna. This was not our political attitude or moral. It wasn't my personal view, because we considered and consider Bosnia-Herzegovina, as one of the people who has lived there for 13 centuries, we consider it our homeland and our state. But as subsequent Washington agreements showed, we were entitled to expect that Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia might create a con-federal union, and that was our political wish, aspiration.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's move on. I'd like the witness to be -- no. Well, let me first ask you some introductory questions. Witness, we are now moving towards July, 1992, and my question is: Do you recall that you were -- that you had a conversation with a journalist in July, 1992, named Marcus Tanner, who is a journalist from the London Independent Service, and do you recall saying to that journalist that you didn't recognise the Bosnian flag or the Bosnian Presidency or a unified Bosnian army? Do you recall saying that to this journalist?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I remember this interview, especially because I did not communicate with journalists much, particularly in view of some of the experience because they never brought the text for my -- to be authorised, to be initialled. And that was also the case with this journalist. I could never lay my hands on this text, so that I would be grateful if you could copy it and give it to me. I can therefore only speak about how I thought and spoke politically at that time. But of course, I cannot record every single word, and I would be grateful also if the journalist had the tape because it would then -- it would have been even more authentic in that case. Therefore, if you think that those speculations need to be denied here, or that they need to be confirmed here, that is of course your position, but I personally can present my thinking now about the point in time and about what I presume -- probably said on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like this article to be shown to the witness so he can read it. Besides, it says that it is Irish Times, as far as I can see, not London. So I believe the Prosecutor should correctly quote document such and such and put it before the witness so the witness can see it. And what we have here is Irish Times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'll show the document to the witness and then we can clarify everything. If the witness can be shown Exhibit P157.3. And this document is in the binder of exhibits which I submitted on Friday. If I can assist the registry, I have a bundle of exhibits here which I'm going to use for this witness which I provided on Friday, but I have an extra copy here so maybe it's easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, the article was in English but we've made a translation into B/C/S for your convenience, so it's being shown to you now and maybe you can read the article. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, yes, of course, but not calmly. That is, I did it superficially which is the only possible way one can read it at this moment, but I can also say that this is just as superficial an approach because it teams with --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Listen to the questions and then you can give your comments to this article. First of all, If you look at the header in response to Mr. Krsnik's question, the document is written by the journalist Marcus Tanner, who is from the London Independent Service, and the article was published in the Irish Times. I hope that will clarify that. Now, Mr. Maric, I'm particularly interested in this -- in this second part of the article which starts in -- with the words, "In Croat-held Jablanica and Konjic." Maybe move up. It starts with, "They point out that the new Croatian zone has not seceded from Sarajevo and that thousands of Muslims in flight from Serbian ethnic cleansing have found sanctuary in Herceg-Bosna. In Croat-held Jablanica and Konjic, I saw thousands of refugees from the east, many dressed in traditional colourful baggy pants, making make shift homes for themselves in former army barracks. But there is no question who runs the shows in Herceg-Bosna. The red and white Croatian checkerboard is more often seen these days than the Bosnian fleur-de-lis. Mr. Mate Boban, the President of Herceg-Bosna, has described the region as Croatian land. In an interview he said, 'Whatever the people in Sarajevo do is their personal business. They cannot speak or decide a thing in the naming of the people of Herceg-Bosna.' His deputy, Mr. Jozo Maric, was harsher: 'We don't recognise the Bosnian flag, the Bosnian Presidency or a unified Bosnian army. They don't have an army in Sarajevo. How can they expect us to place our forces under their control?'" Did you say these words to the journalist, Mr. Tanner?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That is not how I used those words, and to begin with, I was not Mr. Boban's deputy and this merely shows how serious was the journalist and how well he verified his data. I was never Mr. Mate Boban's deputy. So the gentleman opens with a lie, so how could he then transmit, convey my words exactly as I had said them?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mate Boban present at that interview?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was alone in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's move on. Witness, is it correct that your political view of one great Croatia, with all Croats living in one united state, still existed in late 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be crazy, because in 1995, both Dayton and everything else was known, so that somebody might say that if somebody said that, so that he was -- that he was inane so any such statement, taken out of context and quoted, cannot be my view and was not my view, regardless of what kind of a document similar to this one here will produce here or so-called "document," that is a document in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the celebration of the third anniversary of the creation of Ravno Brcko municipality? And this was at the invitation of mayor Mijo Anic and this was held in November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really do not know, are we checking the credibility through statements of 2000, 2002? What does 1995 have to do with the subject of the document except that we know that in 1995, peace was concluded in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Dayton Accords came into force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have the same doubts, but I will let Mr. Bos go to see where he's leading us to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If the witness may be shown Exhibit 802.2, which is also in the binder? It's the next exhibit in the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, you said that you would allow me to comment on the document that we had before. Now, why are you skipping over it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I thought I had given you an opportunity to comment on it but if you want to add something, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just one sentence. I'll read just one sentence. And that is second passage, last sentence, "The new and very quiet border between Croatia and Serbia is in Ilijas on the very edge of Sarajevo, and none of them were asked anything when --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do not know where the witness is reading from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a lie or you are insinuating this -- because no where in this letter from Belgrade or Zagreb and especially Bosnia-Herzegovina ever mentioned about a fictitious or a real border between Croatia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's now move on to the next exhibit, which is Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, which is the number of the document from which he read this last sentence and what document is it and what number does it have?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The document this was still the old exhibit, the article in the Irish Times, Exhibit 157.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, the next document you're going to be shown is an ECMM report and it reports on that meeting which I just have described to you, the university of the creation of Ravne Brcko, and you were present at that meeting and you gave a speech, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I see the speech?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what we have is a -- I don't know if you read English. You can read the report in English or you can read the -- the relevant expert I have translated into B/C/S so you can read the relevant excerpt. Let me go straight to what is relevant here, which is on the paragraph 3 of the report, which -- and the last sentence and it says the following: "The speech of Mr. Jozo Maric was even more radical. 'Who says that Croatia has to be in its former borders? All Croats should live in one united state.'" Witness, is it correct that you stated that in your speech on that evening?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, I do not have that document. I do not know who its author is or what its source is. What I see here is a list of names who are attributed this or that. That is, there are no authentic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We are not talking about authenticity. I'm just asking you whether you said that or not. That's the simple question and you can say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I did not say that. No, I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but the Defence would like to know where this document comes from because the Defence does not have it. Where is the Croatian original? Where did you translate it from? At least that. Because it's a Croatian document, obviously. You must have had it translated from somewhere and the Defence is entitled to know what is this document and where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos, could you give us an explanation on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a report from the European Commission Monitoring Mission, the ECMM, and we've submitted numerous ECMM reports in this case and this is just another ECMM report. And that's why the original is in English and not in B/C/S, and I've translated for Mr. Maric the relevant parts into B/C/S. And it simply reports on a meeting where one of the ECMM representatives was present. That's what the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but at any rate, I'd like to have this whole report, the one from which they took this fragment from. That is, the Defence believes it is entitled to the whole report of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This is the whole report of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, let's move on to another topic, and this concerns the school curricula. Now, you've stated that in the school year 1992-1993, the school curricula and programmes were adapted in a way that the old communist elements, elements that were alien to a democratic society, were removed from the programme; is that correct?.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We endeavoured. We tried to remove, even though it was not simple, to remove what at that time was incompatible with the new democratic trend or rather a new democratic situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you, as chief of the Department of Education, Culture, Sports for the HVO was responsible for the implementation of these new curricula; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really hear quite well your question because of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is it correct that you, as chief of the HVO Department for Education, Culture and Sports, were responsible for the implementation of these new curricula?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was responsible for the adoption of documents, and those who worked on the ground were responsible for their enforcement, and those were teachers in schools, advisors in the institute, and the inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, would you agree with me that the implementation of these new school curricula, that that was an attempt by the HVO to make the school curricula in Herceg-Bosnia the same as in the republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true. I'd really like you to get an expert witness on syllabuses and curricula, and especially a Slavonic expert who would then analyse the curricula, first, of the Republic of Croatia, B, the curricula used in Sarajevo, and C, the curricula and syllabuses of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And that analysis would then bring to light what you are trying to get as an answer or, rather, what is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Witness, do you recall organising a seminar for teachers of all primary and secondary schools in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in December, 1992? The seminar was held on the 5th of December, 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that every school year as of 1992, during the period which is under observation here, we held at least four or five workshops during every school year, and I, as the person responsible for culture, education and so on and so forth, together with the director of the education institute, together with the inspection, and with all the principals, we would participate in those workshops to see how, in view of the difficulties that we were saddled with, we would embark on a new school year. And presumably, this meeting was one in a series of those which I had to convene in my capacity, in order to have the instruction prepared and conducted in the best possible manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 198 -- P198.2? And it's also in the binder. It's the next exhibit in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, is this the invitation for this seminar which is signed by you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not sign this. It was signed, as far as I can see, my secretary, who must have done that in agreement with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. But your name is on there, though, and -- so --

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is true that it is my name here but the signature is -- I will decipher it for you because I know it, and this is Mr. Zeljko Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or "Talic," the interpreters are not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, let's read out -- so this is an invitation for that seminar and it says, "Invitation to a seminar for teachers of the Croatian language, history, geography and physics, which will be held in Dr. Mate Ujevic school centre in Imotski on Saturday, 5 December, 1992, beginning at 9.00 hours." What I'm particularly interested is in the next line, "The seminar will be coordinated by advisors from the education institute of the ministry of the Republic of Croatia." My question is, can you explain to the Trial Chamber what was the role of these advisors from the education institute of the ministry of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can do that, yes. I hope that you've made your inquiries about the jurisdiction of an education institute anywhere in your country or here in the Netherlands. So these are advisors, are experts who monitor the adoption of the curricula, that is, the subjects on which they advise, and then instruct the teachers about the innovations on these subjects under the changed circumstances, with the changed textbooks, how best they will cover them in the classroom. So this is a highly professional specialist subject with no political intrusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And why did these experts come from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, to begin with, at that time, we had a dispersed institute. I mean the institute for instruction and schooling in Mostar. After the -- after the JNA devils laid bear Mostar, there were no people. That is, most people of the Serb ethnicity had already gone and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. remaining Bosnians and Croats were practically not there. So that this institute and this school year was already underway and the institute could not provide a professional analysis and professional instructions, and that is why we continued with the practice that we had from the former Yugoslavia, that these workshops were held in Dubrovnik, in Split, in Istra, where very often the guests were advisors from Zagreb, from elsewhere, from different centres in the former Yugoslavia because why should a subject such as physics, and we know because we all received instruction in it, what kind of political connotations might it hold? Is it the free fall, the Einstein's theory or something? There is nothing that would mean that we had any secret intentions that you seem to be intimating that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, just one more question. Why would you, for example, need advisers on -- from Croatia on the history, on the subject of history? Can you explain that? Or Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in our case, the syllabus and curricula, and I believe it is like that all over the world, all the subjects are equal. This is number 1. For each and every subject, there are adviser. That is, if you wish, they talk about -- if we take language, they talk about the syntax, they speak about the -- look over about choice, they talk about all sorts of things, and the same applies to history, and geography and so on and so forth, so what we wanted was the professional assistance which our teachers needed. In particular, because some of the teachers of these subjects under consideration had left and the scattered all over Europe. And some of these subjects had to be taken over by undergraduates, that is, people who were perhaps in their final years at university but had not graduated and had not taken their examinations in the educational, in teaching subjects, and they needed to be instructed, and that is -- and that is what the advisers in institutes for education are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, we'll move on. Witness, would you agree with me that there was a lot of protests by the Muslims in Herceg-Bosna in 1992 on the manner in which the school programmes and curricula were implemented in 1991 and 1992 and how it was imposed on the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that they complained but those outside the schools, those who had no idea what this was all about, and who had no knowledge of the complexity of school instruction. One of them is a major expert, Mr. Arif Maslic, a military person, who gave instructions to children, to parents and to teachers of Muslim origin in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there were such persons, but competent Muslim teachers and professors, except for the purpose of improving the curricula, never criticised these curricula and school programmes, and they tried to help, together with us, to improve these curricula and programmes for the benefit of all students and pupils, Croat, Muslim and Serb alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you not agree that this Muslim protest must have been based on the fact that they were being discriminated by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as protests that went beyond our normal communication, through the institute, through the ministry, through the principals and headmasters meetings are concerned, so apart from these protests, unless they were instigated by those who had no idea about schools, are something that I never was exposed to and witnessed, but perhaps at certain levels, there were certain criticisms voiced. I certainly cannot be an expert in all individual cases. At the time of war, I could not go to all the territories in which the schools that I was competent for were holding their instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let me just show you some of the type of protests that were made by the Muslims. If the witness can be shown Exhibit P218, please. Witness, this is -- I don't know if you have it in front of you. This is a charter of the Muslims of Herzegovina. It's dated 17 of January 1993. And it's signed by various members of the regional Muslim democratic party and also by Mr. Smajkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. I would like to know whether this document is confidential or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure, but maybe if we can't discuss names and not put it on the ELMO, I think we can discuss the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, let's just look at the content of this document and I would like to refer you to paragraph 2 of this charter and then the last sentence of that paragraph, and I'll read it out to you. "The Muslims of Herzegovina do not accept being transformed from having the status of a people at the beginning of the struggle against the aggressor to an ethnic minority at the end of it, deprived of their elementary ethnic rights in the ordering of their region that is their historical homeland." Let me just make another quote from this document, which is the last sentence of paragraph 3: "As we respect and acknowledge the principle of the equality of all peoples in their right to Bosnia-Herzegovina and the way it is ordered, we demand that the same principle be applied in the ordering of the provinces where it concerns ensuring basic ethnic rights and interests. We demand that this principal is respected consistently in the legislature, in the executive and the judiciary and in other matters of state, as well as in the sphere of education and schooling. Then it continues in paragraph 4, "the Muslims of Herzegovina cannot accept relations and practices that elevate and give supremacy of any one people irrespective of the population of any province it might make up." Witness, would you not agree that this Muslim petition expresses a concern about the equal treatment of Muslims and Croats also in the educational system?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relationship between -- that is towards Croats and Bosniaks, I'll call them Bosniaks, was the same. It was the same because we had curricula and school programmes that did not deny the dignity of either an individual or a people. These curricula and programmes were adopted on the basis of consultations with the Bosniaks who were moratory experts and not like those who are signed here. None of these have a single day of experience in terms of school instruction. These are all officials that were appointed by SDA and youth association, et cetera, so we are again here confronted with people who think that their arguments will become more convincing the higher the number of those who signed the document so we had the same attitude towards both Bosniaks and Croats. There was a balance established here. And the professionals working in the institute for education were both Croats and Bosniaks, principals of schools, headmasters were both Croats and Muslims. In other words, not through a single move did we try to do something to deny anyone, to attack the dignity of a specific people. Particularly in terms of those who were a minority in a particular province, but only in a particular province because in other provinces, they were a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just give you another example, and this is document P244.1, which is also in the binder. My apologies for the quality of the document. It's not very easy to read. But let me read out to you -- I'm particularly interested in paragraph 2 and paragraph 3 of this document. Now, this is a document -- this is an announcement by the president of the Capljina SDA, the executive committee, Mr. Zlatko Bitanga. And the document, although it's difficult to read, is 7 February, 1993. Paragraph 2 reads the following: "The Capljina SDA would like to mention its earlier standpoint that in compliance with the UN conventions, schools, as teaching and training institutions, cannot be used as a place of political activity," and then there is an illegible word, "for any political ideology or government." And then paragraph 3: "The Capljina SDA would like to point out that a school is a multi-ethnic institution and the ethnic or religious feelings of students and teachers should in no way be heard. All of those acting in a school," and then there is some illegible words, "especially the teaching staff, cause the school to stop being what it is supposed to be." Now, Mr. Maric, again, is it not true that this is the type of protest that the Muslim population in Herceg-Bosna made during that period, 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim population did not protest this. If I can read the document well enough, is a protest by Mr. Bitanga, one of the SDA officials, and this is a small segment of the Bosnian Muslims. Even these quotes under items 2 and 3, use conditional tense that it could happen, would happen. It doesn't refer to events that had taken place. They say, "We think that training institutions cannot be used as a place of political activity." In my capacity as the head of the social affairs and education department, I certainly did my best to make sure that political activity never be included in any activities in the school. Now, if you have documents which would show that we imposed something on teachers, professors, that we inserted something into the curricula and programmes that would hurt the feelings of anyone, then you should show them to me. This, however, is obviously a political document issued by a party which at that time was very much against a part of the Croat policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, let's move this document aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we break here?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Bring in the witness, please. Sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, on Friday, you were shown a couple of exhibits by the Defence which were letters from Mr. Arif Pasalic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that when you were shown those documents, that that was the first time that you ever saw those documents?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're not in a position to authenticate those documents, are you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even try to speak about the authenticity of those documents. What I spoke about was something which is much more important than the authenticity. The authenticity is something that you'll confirm, namely, that an officer at a moment in which no competent Ministry of Education --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm cutting you off. I'm just asking you whether you can authenticate, and you can simply say "yes" or "no," and in this case, I suppose you would have to say no, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once you allow me to make comments, then on other situations you don't, but to answer your question, as far as these documents are concerned, and given the fact that I'm not an expert that could establish their authenticity, cannot say whether they are authentic or not, because I'm not an expert in this area, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Exactly. And that was my question and it could have been answered with a simple answer, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit D1/104, which is one of these Pasalic letters? We are just waiting for the exhibit. I have here an extra copy, if that may help.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, is it correct that you were shown this document on Friday?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct, because we don't have an English translation of this document, but is it correct that this is a letter of Mr. Arif Pasalic dated 23 March, 1993, which relates to the closing of the university in Mostar and the relocation of certain faculties to Neum and Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I speak about facts that have to do with the university in 1992-93, in the school year 1992-93. Because of war conflicts in Mostar, which you and Their Honours probably have examined thoroughly well, it was not possible to organise, particularly in the demolished buildings, to organise instruction either in the elementary school, secondary schools and particularly not in the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: My question was whether this letter talks about this and I think it requires a simple answer, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic, in this letter that I have in my hands, speaks about something that he's not familiar about, namely about the confiscation of the property of the faculties, which is not true. And somebody who is not competent in these matters and does not understand them cannot speak correctly, if of course this is a correct and authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So is it correct that in paragraph 1, that Mr. Pasalic complains that the old Mostar university had ceased to exist and that a whole new university was created and that the Croatian language was introduced at the university and that there was a whole new university law? Is that in fact what he's stating in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of these three subquestions you put to me is correct. The university in Mostar was not abandoned. It continued to work. But because of wartime circumstances, the demolished buildings, it had to, on a temporary basis, to be relocated. As to the language of instruction in which lectures were held, each professor used the language that he or she spoke until then, and the same applies to the language which was used by the students in their exams. So Mr. Pasalic does not understand these matters at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that in paragraph 2 of this letter, Mr. Pasalic states that the Muslim student population of the universities of Mostar had dropped down to less than 20 per cent as a result of these changes?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he got this piece of statistics concerning either an increase or a decrease in the number of students. You could establish this through the documentation of each of these faculties, whenever enrolment is made, statistics are compiled. Therefore, without these documents that would be provided by individual faculties and the chancellor's office, this is an invented figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Let's move on. Witness, beside being responsible for the education in 1992 and 1993, were you also chief and later minister of the HVO department of culture?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you referring to in your question?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From November or December, 1992, as I said before, onward, I was the head of the subdepartment of education, culture and sports in the department of social affairs. From 1993 onward, my official position was a minister in the Ministry of Education, School, Culture and Sport of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you agree that during this period, that you held this function, that a lot of Muslim cultural heritages such as numerous mosques were intentionally destroyed by the HVO, either destroyed or heavily damaged?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying that the HVO didn't destroy any mosques or damage any mosques in their war against the Muslims? Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what happened and how the damage was done, but I presume that the Prosecutor has the book entitled, "The Urbicide in the city of Mostar" and you will have noticed that out of 14 mosques in the city of Mostar, only two remain undamaged. Out of five mosques, only two remained undamaged. So 12 mosques were damaged and destroyed by the JNA and the Serbs. Out of ten bridges in Mostar, nine were destroyed, including the old bridge. And of course, cultural institutions and others, even of their own people, namely the Serbs, were demolished. I hope you won't mind my giving you this book, which is in English, in Italian and in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. German, and it contains the evidence of what was going on and what was demolished in Mostar from 1992 until the clashes between the Croats and the Muslims that broke out in 1993. Here you go, sir. This is your copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, we are not discussing whether mosques were also destroyed by the Serbs, and I'll take your word for that, but my question is were mosques also destroyed by the HVO? Would you give an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will tell you that the HVO was not destroying the mosques. The individuals on the basis of their own will and initiative have committed this cultural crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So it's your statement that the HVO never damaged or destroyed any Muslim mosque in the war against the Muslims in 1992 and 1993? That is your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not my statement. It was very clearly and concisely that I said that the HVO, and I'm referring to its civilian part, and I'm also referring to those military parts that I am familiar with, never had either an order or strategy of destroying institutions of culture. Whether the individuals have done this, well, that I know happened indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you do know that certain mosques were destroyed? Whether it was on an order or not, mosques were destroyed in that period?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that churches were destroyed, were damaged. I know that institutions of culture and mosques were destroyed because this cultural and architectural heritage of -- was destroyed, namely, those that belonged to these people and these peoples down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying that you knew that mosques were destroyed. Let me ask you, in your position as Minister of HVO or chief of the department, what did you do to stop this damaging and destruction of cultural heritage? And I'm now particularly referring to the mosques that were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you see that I'm not reacting, that I'm letting it go, but my objection is that the witness -- the witness has answered one and the same question four times and explained it very well. I wasn't checking the English language but he answered the Prosecutor's question four times, loudly and clearly, saying that if some individuals had done that, individuals, independent, autonomous, individuals - I don't know what the English interpretation was - and he answered clearly four times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, the question put by the Prosecution is that, in your position as Minister of HVO or chief of the department, what did you do to stop those damage and destructions of cultural heritage? I don't think the witness answered this question yet. Let us hear the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour, but I believe that the witness has been testifying for two days about his role and he was in the civilian sector, and the question was the HVO military sector. He is the Minister of Education - of education - and he has been testifying for two days already, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we want to hear what the witness is going to tell us, not the answer by you. Witness, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I, as a Minister of Education, Culture and Sports, at the regular consultations that I had with my subordinates, and in the area of culture, these are the heads of non-production activities and individual municipalities, that is, people who at municipal level took care of monuments of culture. To them, I gave explicit instructions, directives, that they had to see to it in their respective areas that the monuments of culture and history be protected, and I requested from them regular reports from the ground about any monument of culture or history from the Roman times, and there were many such monuments up to the 20th century. So I explicitly requested from them and told them that they had to act as much as possible, that they should act by marking, by protecting, that is monuments of history and culture, architectural ones in the first place. The second thing I did, at government sessions of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, later on the Croat -- excuse, me the Croat republic Herceg-Bosna, I requested ministers concerned in the government, that is those covering the area where there was a war, that is the ministry of the police, the minister of the army, I said that they had to do everything in line with the conventions on the protection of the monuments of history and culture and heritage, and it can be done because you must have come by all the documents. One can read it in the minutes, in the records of the government sessions of the Croat community Herceg-Bosna, and subsequently the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So these were the two avenues that I took. The third thing I did -- unfortunately, we have an institute for the protection of monuments which is not sufficiently professional and not sufficiently equipped, but straight away, we sent to the field, wherever it was possible, we sent photographs, art historians, people responsible for conservation, to take photographs, and in line with what could be done at the time, to try to conserve or protect damaged monuments. That is what was done with the series of monuments which we tried to cover with the plastic foil, to protect them in other way, to store the moveable treasures from churches, from libraries and from museums. So these are the most important activities which I undertook as the minister concerned so as to protect the cultural and historical treasures, regardless what people it belonged to. And after the war, that is 1995, a part of what we had stored and protected we exchanged and took back to the place or to the owners that it belonged to, be it the Islamic religious community, be it the Serb Orthodox Church, or some institutions such as museums, libraries and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying that you actually did talk to the HVO Ministry of army as you call it and that you expressed your concerns to him? Is that correct? And did any --

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. It is correct. At the sessions of the government, I warned that since there are people whose awareness is not high enough to protect the artistic treasures, yes, it is true that I spoke about that at the government meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What was the response of the minister and did the situation improve?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministers concerned, and it was one of the government conclusions, was that the ministers concerned will have to undertake everything within their jurisdiction to protect it, and that is what they -- that they were tasked with at the sessions and meetings of the government and the government conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to avoid any framing, I'd like the Prosecutor to tell us what mosques he has in mind because the witness has already said that of the mosques, 12 were destroyed by the Serbs, so what mosques, what other monuments, is the Prosecutor talking about and blaming the HVO for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not intending to go into a discussion of which mosques, I'm just talking generally whether mosques were destroyed or damaged and I don't want to go into this discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I believe that your witness has answered your question in a very good way. We could get a very clear picture on what happened in this situation. I understand that the Prosecution is not aiming at incriminalising your witness at all. He just wants to know the policy of certain organisations at that time. I believe your witness is quite capable in this field. Let's move on and not stop at those very details. This is not the very subject of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. I do not know -- I see there is more and more misunderstanding in interpretation because I hear what the witness is saying and then I hear the Prosecutor's questions regarding the spirit of the language. If the witness answers the question and then the Prosecutor asks five or six questions about the destruction of I don't know how many mosques after the witness has answered what he could answer about, and then again in his questions he tells the witness that this has reached, I don't know what proportions, after the witness has said, and answered the question about the mosques. It is intimated that this has acquired I don't know what proportions because, Your Honours, I bring here witnesses on the basis of the indictment who will testify about whether my client did something or not, rather than have the Prosecutor's Office conduct investigations here because they could have conducted the investigation before this case, and all the future witnesses will only be testifying on the basis of the indictment regarding my client. I will not allow anyone to conduct investigations here or collect information under the guise of credibility. If something was done in Mostar, then the Prosecutor will have to prove that it was done by my client and I will bring witnesses who will show whether he did it or did not. I will not bring anybody else and that is my chief objection. After the witness answered that of 14 mosques, 12 were destroyed by Serbs, look at all the questions that followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the Prosecution is agreed that we should move on at this point. Yes, Mr. Bos. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Maric I just have a couple of questions left for you. Witness, do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you have any sons?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two sons and two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did any of your sons serve in the army, in the conflict against either the Serbs or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My sons are too young. The older one was born in 1978 and long after the end of the conflict, he did his regular military service, that is two or three years ago and they are both university students.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination? Mr. Krsnik? Re-examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's first address this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, could you please give me this book? I'm just asking my colleague to find the Defence number because it will be our -- the exhibit that we intend to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Tell us, does this book describe in detail all the devastation, the destruction of monuments of culture in the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the destruction is described in detail and it is done competently because it was done by the most competent experts on history, culture, architecture and town planning and monument protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Since somewhere under the UNESCO protection if there were such, were they verified at the international level?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the book was verified internationally because institutions were in Mostar responsible for the maintenance of institutions of cultures from the protection to the description and so on and so forth. And it involved both Bosnians and Croats as one can see here from the credits list. That is authors, expert studies and the expert team which prepared the whole book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please put on the ELMO this photograph here, just as an example?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Tell us, what do we see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recognise, because it is a detail of this monument, this is the Mostar secondary school, it's name was Alexa Santic before the war until 1992. So there is the first secondary school in Mostar, that is its facade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was it hit by a shell or let me not ask you leading questions. When did it stop working, when did they start working or did they start working again?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it stopped working immediately because instruction could not be provided in it because both the roof and the openings and the interior were destroyed and, well, I stand to be corrected, its reconstruction started only two or three years ago and some instruction is taking part in it, that is the whole building has not been open yet fully because it has not been reconstructed either in --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Will you please tell us the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's too fast, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I get carried away because we speak the same language and believe me that it might happen to you, too. You simply get carried away. My apologies to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why don't you look at the screen? It will be easier for you to see when the interpretation ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are quite right, Your Honour, I shall try to do that because it is of course in my interests that the interpretation is as good and as precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: First I'd like to ask you, sir, Mr. Maric, will you read which page it is?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is page 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, no, no, the pages.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The page is 135 and the photograph is number 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Please give us the full title of the book.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The book is called, "Mostar 1992 Urbicide." "Urbis" means city. So this is a new linguistic coinage, that is the destruction of a city.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Will you tell us who the publisher is? It should be somewhere in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a public enterprise for the reconstruction and construction of Mostar. So "Urbing" is an acronym, Urba, "Urbis," that is, and "Eng," engineer, so this is a public enterprise responsible for town planning and construction and all that is relevant for the functioning, construction and protection of a city and its architectural and town planning values.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Will you now turn the first page and tell us which the exhibit number? It's on the first page. This is the exhibit number, isn't it? ID D --

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, this yellow thing that I stuck on. So the book's number would be?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is 131.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That is D/ what?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Slash" 131. I don't understand this acronym so I can't really --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I only wanted -- all I wanted was to have the number of this exhibit read out, which you wrote on this book. Mr. Maric, will you please be so kind and have the usher give you IAC number 2. I apologise, I forgot to ask you -- you said the two mosques remained standing. Have you heard of their being destroyed or damaged by some individuals who acted on their own?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they remained intact, that is after the JNA conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where were those mosques?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roznavedzi and Ibrahim Efendijina. I don't know where they are because I have never lived in Mostar to know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You have the document in front of you, document marked IAC-2. Tell me, the terminology as is used at the beginning of this document, Croat regional community or Travnik regional community, did it ever exist? Did such terminology ever exist?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To arrive at individual, official names and especially the socio-political organisation at the state level, it must be adopted by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relevant bodies. So such terminology, Herzegovina regional community, Travnik regional community, did not exist because I do not remember, either in the state and legal organisation of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or later on in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I do not remember that such terminology existed and, in particular, that it had been legally verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you see in this document any handwritten signature by anyone?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no signatures here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And tell me, you, as the mayor, that is the first man of the municipality of Grude, do you ever -- let me put it this way. Would it be humiliating for you to keep -- to keep records, to be a recording clerk?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always went by what was normal, usual, in the communication in business, that is business correspondence, as we put it professionally, to know exactly where is whose place and who does what. So I, as the municipal mayor, the mayor of the municipal assembly, I had men who had been verified, in terms of their education and the place where they worked, to do -- to do individual jobs. So that we had technical recording clerks who were legally educated, who could not let any error slip by or, at least, who could know how to keep errors down to a minimum in cases of such correspondence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me ask you more specifically, did you as the mayor ever keep the record?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because that was not my job. I had to conduct -- I had to chair the meetings and somebody else kept the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So tell us, will you please comment on this document? Do you have any idea who could have written this? Where does this come from?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that this was done by somebody who really knows very little about business correspondence and correspondence in general, because had that been the case, then at least this document would have been all right from the point of view of the legal form, and it is not in conformity with it. When we correspond, the preamble or rather the title, which says, "Herzegovina regional community" and underneath and down there, at the bottom, it said, "Regional Crisis Staff for Herzegovina." So how can we have one institution above and another one where the signature should be? So this is an obvious proof of a forgery, of a counterfeit document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to Exhibit P157.3. Let me ask you first, do you know if this journalist ever spoke with Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, but, yes, he did speak with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: With Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, simply because Mr. Boban had a different type of communication with journalists, and I was completely separate from it so that, even physically, I had no way of knowing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Will you please look at page 2 and read the first two sentences?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the top, the very top?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, where it says, "Mr. Mate Boban."

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mr. Mate Boban, President of Herceg-Bosna, describes the region as the Croat land, and in one interview," I guess this is a misprint, "Stated whatever people in Sarajevo do, it's up to them. They cannot speak or decide anything on behalf of people of Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So tell us, do these two sentences mean that this journalist ever spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the journalist exerted himself and reached Mr. Boban, then presumably, he got a whole interview from him and Mr. Mate Boban, who was very -- a very public figure, would have probably -- presumably given an whole interview rather than just a few sentences taken out of something else. So I, who also cooperated with newspapers, would have used it. That is a man who at that time was a negotiator in the international community, I wouldn't have accorded him half a sentence, because this either testifies to the lack of professionalism or the lack of authenticity of what this journalist is writing about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When answering Mr. Bos's question, my learned friend, you said that this journalist 0 and I cannot remember which sentence you had in mind - you said that he was not telling the truth or, rather, that he did not write the truth.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a series of passages in the first part which seems to indicate that the journalist in question presumably did not look right. For instance, if he moved between Grude and Sarajevo, that it was not the result of what he saw but what others had possibly told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In the beginning of this text, it says, "The Croatian soldiers are busy forging a roughly made two-track highway through the mountains to link the Croatian town -- the Croat towns of central Bosnia with the sea. The men in charge of the work wear the uniforms of the HVO." This text was written on the 13th of July, 1992. What kind of road was being built on the 13th of July, 1992, in central Bosnia of all places?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no clear geographic location, no exact coordinates of the area that he is referring to, so I could read it -- I could read that it could be in Karakorum or somewhere in the Himalayas, rather than in Herzegovina because those who took that road, indeed, it does not really look as flat as the Netherlands but it's not all the rocks and ravines. It is quite true that at that time a number of roads were being built and one of them -- one of those that the journalist has in mind could be that road, but perhaps it would be best for him to explain, if he were here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Weren't those roads -- excuse me. Are you familiar with the term, "The road of salvation"?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well as far as I know in the history of warfare, in war conflicts first one endeavours to take over the routes. The JNA managed to take over the communications between Mostar and Sarajevo and so in order to send humanitarian or any other assistance, some alternate routes had to be found.
