Frequently, they went through rougher -- they cut across -- they went across rougher terrain so one tried to improvise, they tried to make do somehow but they had been neglected so one could meet the basic necessities of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you, as a high official at the time, do you know that it was the refugees from central -- from west -- from eastern Bosnia and central Bosnia from the areas attacked by the JNA that those roads were taken by all the Croat and Muslim population who had to flee from those areas?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because as mayor I had to organise the accommodation of those roads described from west Bosnia from central Bosnia, from east Bosnia partly also during the conflicts of Croatia some people from west Bosnia came to Herzegovina, but at the time that this article refers to these are mostly refugees from east Bosnia, that is those who are moving towards west Herzegovina and on towards Croatia and Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The last quote from this article:" Bosnia has been disappearing and is dying, torched and uprooted by the Serbs in eastern Bosnia, painlessly snuffed out by the Croats in the southwest. The old Bosnia, the ethnic mosaic of the Croats, Serbs and Muslims, has shrunk to a few square miles inside Sarajevo. 13 July of 1992 is when this was written down?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who are familiar with facts will find it ridiculous that Bosnia has shrunk to a few square miles inside Sarajevo. Well Sarajevo has about 400.000 inhabitation from Stup to Bistrik it stretches over about 10 to 12 kilometres, so this is the longitudinal line and then the cross line, the horizontal line of about 3 to 4 kilometres and it is really ridiculous for somebody to it speak about Bosnia-Herzegovina and the ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992. This is simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Did you ever -- have you ever authorised this interview?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The journalist had promised to me to send it for me to authorise and later on to send me the paper in which it would be published but I cannot recall him ever doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'll read to you once again your alleged comment but before that, I'll put the second -- the next question to you. Is there a Bosnian flag? Is there a Bosnian coat of arms with a sickle and a moon in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July, 1992, about 70 per cent of Bosnia are occupied by Serbs, Sarajevo is under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is there a Bosnian flag?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no Bosnian flag that would have been approved and adopted and embraced by all three peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Couldn't then that have been a flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have been a flag approved by the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Having published an announcement, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would that flag be called the flag of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The official name was the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina until the start of the war, and later on Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, tell me, at that time, the same date, July 1992, was there a common Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, there existed no common Bosnian-Herzegovinian army. I've noted your wording and I'm being very specific. There is no Bosnian-Herzegovinian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: These are not my words. I'm quoting the journalist.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well I'm telling you what I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Since you answered the Prosecutor's question that you never had said that, I will not continue. Let us proceed to Exhibit P802.2. 802.2. I have two questions. When were the Dayton Accords signed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact date? Well, it was signed in 1994, the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, have a look at this document, the date. Here you have your alleged statements about the establishment of Ravne-Brcko. The date is November 5, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the document be put on the ELMO, please? The interpreters don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you please put this document on the ELMO, at the request of the interpreters? Tell me, on the 5th of November, what would be the purpose for me to once again say, having the knowledge that the Dayton Accords had been signed, who says that Croatia has to be within a single -- within the borders of a single state, all Croats should live within a unified state? My question is, did you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What would be the purpose of such a sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the observers would have to be asked whether this is what they heard, whether the interpreter with them did a good job, and whether they have a recording of that. I personally never said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed. Do you perhaps know what was the percentage with which SDA won in Mostar and Herzegovina, with what percentage of votes?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is the SDA an exclusive party that can represent and speak on behalf of all Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina or Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I am an advocate of a multi-party system, and I believe that every party - and this is a fact of truth and history - this was a multi-party entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Exhibit P244.1 is something that prompted me to put you this question. My first question: Were you at the ministry exposed to any complaints by the parents of the students and pupils? Have you received any complaint, in 1992-93, from the parents of the schools that you were competent for concerning curricula and school programmes?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I received no complaint either waged by parents or the competent people in the corpus of the Bosnian people, and I'm referring to the institute of education, the Ministry of Education, that was operating in Sarajevo, and I'm also referring to principals and headmasters of the schools, as well as the parents who also could have voiced their displeasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, this announcement, do you know where it was published?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this announcement. It is the first time that I have seen it, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The announcement is signed by?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President -- the President of the Capljina SDA, Mr. Bitanga, Zlatko.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In English, it says Satko.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In the English translation, and I will go very slowly, it says, S-a-t-k-o, Satko Bitanga. So Satko is the first name, Bitanga is the family name. In the Croatian original, however, the name is quite illegible, first name, that is. Therefore, again my question: Have you ever heard of somebody called Satko Bitanga?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard much a person who is signed here, whatever his real name, whatever the name should be written or pronounced. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: As far as these other documents are concerned, the learned friend did not cross-examine you on them. Therefore I'm not allowed to do it either. Therefore, Mr. Maric, I'd like to thank you very much for answering our invitation to come here and help us all to hear your testimony. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you all. Thank you to Their Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from Judges? Judge Diarra, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, I have two questions for you. The Prosecutor asked you if Mr. Kljuic was accused by Herceg-Bosna because he agreed to cooperate with Muslims, and that his cooperation has also brought certain Croats under the Muslims, subordinated them to Muslims, placed them under the orders of Muslims. But I did not quite understand your answer. Was it yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not hear the name, Your Honour, and the interpreters told us that they could not hear the name that you used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry if I deform those names.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please, once again, very clearly specify the question? What exactly do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor asked you if Kljujic had been accused because he accepted to cooperate with Muslims, and he was mostly reproached for having allowed to put the Croats under the orders of Muslims, and the Prosecutor asked you if that was true and if Mr. Kljujic was accused by Herceg-Bosna, because he agreed to cooperate with Muslims, and that his cooperation has also brought a certain Croats under the Muslims, subordinated them to Muslims, placed them under the orders of Muslims. But I did not quite understand your answer. Was it yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not hear the name, Your Honour, and the interpreters told us that they could not hear the name that you used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry if I deform those names.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please, once again, very clearly specify the question? What exactly do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor asked you if Kljujic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had been accused because he accepted to cooperate with Muslims, and he was mostly reproached for having allowed to put the Croats under the orders of Muslims, and the Prosecutor asked you if that was true and if Mr. Kljujic was indeed accused by some people in Herceg-Bosna or the HVO. Was your answer yes or -- yes, it happened, or no, it did not happen, because it was -- because your answer was so fast that I did not catch it. If I am misquoting the Prosecutor, perhaps he could help me, because it was really very fast. The witness was so fast that my head was spinning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If you wish, I have it in front of me what I put to this witness and I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, please do that, and I want to hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What I had stated to you, Mr. Maric is the following: Is it not true that during that meeting, several Bosnian Croats, and especially from the region of Herceg-Bosna, openly accused Mr. Kljujic for being a traitor of the Croatian interests because he cooperated with the Muslim party and brought the Croats into an inferior position? That's what I had put to Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my answer, I said that politically, I disagreed with Mr. Kljujic. We disagreed with Mr. Kljujic and we put it very openly and that we, as a party throughout this time, at political and practical levels, we cooperated with the Muslims, to an extent to which we thought that such cooperation can benefit both peoples and can benefit the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was then manifested in a variety of our contacts, moves and meetings. Being an organised party, we insisted that the president of the party, who was also a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on behalf of this party, cannot act on his own without the support of the party body, i.e., without the Presidency or without the central board of the party, without the two supreme political bodies of the party. So I'm referring to the main, central board, the main board comprising 50 members or more that could pass political decisions and then the Presidency, the executive body. Mr. Kljujic, on his own, without any consultation with the Presidency and the main board, made certain steps and this is what we objected, and this was an intra-party conflict and not a conflict which was waged against the Bosnian Muslims. We believed it a legitimate move to discuss each member of the party and to compel every member of the party to abide by the decisions and the strategies of the main board and the Presidency of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I understand. Yes. The Prosecutor also asked you if you remember stating some day that you would never accept to subordinate yourself to the authority of the Turks, referring to the Bosnian Muslims, and your answer was, I believe, that is possible that you had made that statement. Can you confirm this answer or is it that I did not get your answer because of the speed with which you speak?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the authenticity of that meeting and the minutes of the statements made there, I already testified about that. Let me repeat that the Croat Democratic Union, and I myself, had one attitude towards the Muslim people and a different attitude towards the individuals who were the top ranking SDA officials. In the SDA, there were people who were extremist fundamentalists in their orientations, who demanded in Sarajevo that women, once again, start wearing the veil covering their face and a lot of other things which, when in 1888 had been abandoned in Bosnia when the Austro-Hungarian monarchy was established. I disagreed with this and you should know that Bosniaks, members of other political parties, also disagreed with this type of practices. And this can be seen through the heated debates in the parliament, in the media, et cetera. I wanted to emphasise that we cannot go back into the 19th century but that rather, like all other parts of modern Europe, we have to go forward. We could not use as models some Middle East countries that were bringing back their women to the Middle Ages, not just women but also their schools and a lot of other things that had belonged to the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the question was, did you really say Muslim fundamentalists, that is one thing, but if you used the word "Turk," that it means that in your subconscious prevails the opinion that the Muslims are Turks. And that is something which is not a good basis for peace.

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, the expression "Turks" is not something that you can understand in the ethnic terms and make it equal to the current population of Turkey today or their ethnic communities that lived outside Turkey, including Macedonia and Kosovo. As far as I know, according to the population census, I hardly believe that a single person committed them or announced them as members of the Turkish ethnicity. I was in fact referring to Turks in the widest ethnic term, but the man on the street, in his everyday language, sometimes would equalise the Catholics with Rome, the members of the orthodox church with Istanbul, and the Muslims with the Turks. This is what the less educated part of our population would do. And there were no insulting elements in using this type of language. It was just the popular, colloquial way of expressing by less well educated individuals. So the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina were sometimes referred to as the Latin people; the Serbs or the Orthodox Church members as the Byzantine people, the people from Istanbul, and until the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this had no insulting connotation whatsoever. It is only during the war, when tensions developed, these words were given a different connotation, a pejorative meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you do not come from the grassroots. You are very educated. You have a very high degree of education. But thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, any questions out of Judges' questions? Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my last question. Further examination by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that meeting, did you say Turks or not?

utterances.speaker: JOZO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not say Turks. It should be quite clear because I'm familiar with this distinction, linguistic and otherwise, which is more sensitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very. Thank you, Witness, for coming here to help us. We all wish you good luck in your future. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We understand that both parties submitted some lists for the exhibits to be used in the direct and the cross-examinations but now we want to have lists of those documents you are going to tender through the witnesses, including from the first witness to now. We understand that we are not in a position to admit all those witnesses because of the translation but we've got guarantees from the Registrar, those translations will follow up for the next witness. Yes, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, with regard to this witness, Your Honour, I introduced five new exhibits and I think all of them were in the English language, so I think I can list them now and I can ask whether they can be admitted or not for this particular witness. I have them here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bos, my suggestion is that you submit the list to us and to the other parties, and we could not admit your exhibits before we admitted the exhibits tendered from the Defence counsel. Shall we do it all together?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If that's your wish, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik. It's the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll ask for only one minute before the new witness is being brought in, something concerning the new documents and the videotapes. I followed my promise. Mr. Meek and myself, we went through a lot of transcripts over the weekend and we took note of the rulings made by the Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll break until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Very briefly, the Defence is kindly requesting of this Court that new documents, those about to be introduced through cross-examination, be disclosed to the Defence prior to the cross-examination. We must familiarise ourselves with them. And the same goes for videotapes. When we had Bozo Rajic, we then saw the tape the very minute that it was shown. We looked through the transcript, and when I introduced a tape with witness Seid Smajkic, the Prosecutor requested to see it, he got it, he went through it. You remember the situation. I spent a whole night translating, and so on and so forth. So I do not think that the Defence can see the tape, we are even not given before the solemn declaration. We saw it only when it was run during the cross-examination. The same goes for new documents. Of course, those other documents which had already been admitted, we know them and they present no difficulty, but when it comes to new documents, we believe the Defence needs to be acquainted with them and your decision was at the time when I was cross-examining, and there are several decisions, and what I quote in the motion that I filed this morning, your ruling was -- and you addressed me, Mr. Seric and me. When we conducted our cross-examination, we were told that we had to submit all the material before the beginning of the trial. [In English] Before the trial. [Interpretation] And I'd like to ask the Honourable Court to extend the same ruling to the Prosecution, nothing more and nothing less. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, first I want to make sure clear that I don't pretend to have recently gone back and made an exhaustive review of the transcript so I allow for the possibility that anything I'm about to say could be wrong based upon going back and making a detailed analysis of the transcript since September. Certainly, I haven't done that. However, I think the case is this: What we've understood the Court's rulings to be in terms of the documents to be used on cross-examination is that when the witness is tendered for cross-examination, if you will, when direct examination is completed and he's now becoming a witness for cross-examination, we understood the Chamber's ruling to be that we would provide a list of the documents to be used, and that's what we have been doing. In some cases, some of the documents maybe also be going over at that time. But as we've said before, sometimes the documents continue to be discovered in the course of preparing for cross-examination as we hear the witness, even on cross-examination, give answers. And so -- sorry, I'll slow down. In any event, Your Honour, our position, our understanding, has been that we are complying with the Chamber's rulings by providing the list which we have been doing with the past several witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for this issue this Trial Chamber has made several decisions orally before, even in the Prosecution's case in chief. I don't believe there is a need for us to repeat the decisions we have made and we also believe that these rulings are applicable to both parties, that is, we asked both parties to submit a list of the exhibits they are going to use in the cross-examination before their cross-examination, for the purpose of facilitating the proceedings. There is no substantial changes of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and there is no substantial changes of the rules concerning cross-examination. This Trial Chamber will make decisions after we were seized by the motions filed by Defence counsel on this very issue. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I merely wanted your decision with regard to videotapes, and I do not think it is fair and just, first, because the Defence did not do it when it was in such a position with regard to videotapes. We needed to see what these videotapes are about prior to the examination rather than during the cross-examination, because I did that when I conducted the cross-examination, in conformity with your decision, and the order that you gave to the Prosecutor, we studied it in detail, there was dispute whether it would be prior or after the solemn declaration by witnesses. But whatever the case, we need to be given in the morning of the day when the solemn declaration is made. Our learned friends do not go by it and still they do it right before the beginning of the cross-examination. The Defence was not in the same position when it conducted cross-examinations. Thank you. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We believe that the videotapes, if used as an exhibit, should be treated as equally as with other exhibits. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President, just one follow-up to the last point. Bozo Rajic is the witness that I cross-examined. We had not only the videotape but we had also made a translation or I should say a transcript of what he said on the videotape. The transcript was provided to the defence, certainly the morning of the day in which the videotape was shown, if not earlier, because all of the Bozo Rajic exhibits that we intended to use or thought we might use in the cross-examination of that witness were all provided to the Defence, not just a list but the exhibits themselves, were all provided to the Defence before the cross-examination started, and they had the transcript of the videotape well before the videotape was shown to the witness. So I just wanted to make that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your clarification is in the record. Well, Mr. Krsnik, would you please brief us on the protective measures of the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness has applied for protective measures, that is a pseudonym and face distortion, because he still lives and works in the area and for the other reasons that I have already indicated in our submissions and motions that I filed with the Honourable Court, and principally, and we have already -- we have written it, we have also received the translations of newspaper articles that we have filed, I think not only this witness but a vast majority of the witnesses who were ready to testify in public now do not want to because the journalists drag them all over the newspapers and misrepresent their testimonies before this Court, working for this or that lobby and thus disturb their families and themselves and that is one of the reasons, and you will see with the articles that we translated, you will see from these articles how much intimidation is placed through newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I would note, Mr. President, that the last or the most -- the latest list of Defence witnesses and witness summaries that were submitted on the 4th of April had this witness testifying publicly. No, we don't object to the witness has evidently changed his minds and now wants these protective measures. We don't object to that although I don't think that that should be taken as some concession on our part that because of what's being said or written in the various media, I wouldn't want there to be any -- anyone wondering whether that's somehow attributed to the Prosecution or something that we can control at all which of course we can't. We don't object to the requested protective measures for this witness. However, before he starts, Mr. President, I would like to very briefly put into the record the state of things with respect to our hearing this witness today. Because we do feel that we are in a significant disadvantage in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. terms of cross-examination. The Trial Chamber made a ruling or a decision last Friday afternoon which resulted in two previous witnesses being sent home, and recognising that that decision was the result of a motion filed by the Prosecution, however, apparently the Defence was informed that the witnesses were being sent home. Obviously the Trial Chamber knew. I think the registry, certainly the victim and witnesses section knew. No one informed us and a significant amount of time was spent this weekend preparing for those two witnesses that were being sent back without our knowledge. And apart from the colossal waste of time that that brought about over the weekend, it also puts us in a more difficult situation now in terms of our preparation for this witness, and I would only ask that we be notified or that the Trial Chamber make sure that the Prosecution is notified when changes of this nature are made. Because no one told us, Mr. President, and we didn't know and we acted on the basis of the previous witnesses being here when we worked this weekend. Now, I can say that a list, a revised list, was sent by fax into our offices Friday afternoon at around 4.30 from the Defence. The fax was sent to Mr. Scott, whom the Defence knew wasn't here on Friday. We saw the fax this morning when Mr. Scott came into the office and got a look at the incoming documents that had come in for him. Not a phone call from the Defence. Not any sort of notice from the Defence, which would have put us on notice that in fact this change had been ordered by the Trial Chamber. So we didn't know until this morning that this witness would be appearing today. Secondly, we don't have a witness summary for this witness under 65 ter(G). As the Trial Chamber will know, the first Defence submissions on witness summaries were made on the 15th of March, and after that time, the Trial Chamber directed the Defence to provide more detailed information, more detailed witness summaries. Those summaries were filed on the 21st of March. However, those more detailed witness summaries covered only what the Defence at that time was saying would be their first ten witnesses. The next witness who is going to start his testimony in a couple minutes is not to be found on those revised, more detailed witness summaries that were submitted on the 21st of March. So for this witness, not only did we not know he was testifying until this morning, we also still have only a very brief, general, useless witness summary, the one that was filed originally by the defence back in March. We've never gotten more information about what he's going to say and for that reason we feel that we are doubly disadvantaged as a result of his beginning his testimony this morning. So I know that the Trial Chamber has made a ruling that the other witnesses were to go home. This witness is here. I'm not asking that he not testify this morning, but I did want the Trial Chamber to know that the circumstances are such that we do feel that we are confronting some significant disadvantages in our preparations for cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- no. We don't want to spend much time on debate on this issue. This issue has been raised at the beginning of today by Mr. Scott already. First thing is about the protective measures of the next witness. Since there is no significant objections from the Prosecution, your request, Mr. Krsnik, for the protective measures has been granted. Secondly, as I said before, that issue has been raised and we have discussed it already. The views expressed by the Prosecution is taken in the record. Thirdly, as for the next witness, if the Prosecution is not satisfied with the summaries of the next witness, they may raise it at any time to the attention to this Trial Chamber and to the Defence party on that. I hope that both parties will meet together to consult with each other concerning any disagreement and problem occurred during the proceedings. Since time is very precious, we will have the next witness. Mr. Usher, will you please bring in the next witness, please? Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I merely wish to bring it to your attention that the Defence has complemented its summaries and that we have sent them. We gave them to our distinguished case manager, Ms. Fleming, completely new summaries which we amplified, extended, working over the weekend, complying with your rule. We have added new facts to them and extended them. If our learned friends are not happy then even with that, then of course we can hold another meeting. Your Honours, I also wish to bring to your attention another matter that I have -- that I was notified about during the break in view of your decision with regard to these two witnesses. We have two witnesses who arrived here, but the second witness is in the hospital for the second day here in The Hague, and if the state of his health deteriorates, I was informed that he went to the hospital -- that he was in the hospital yesterday again, with the intervention of the service for the protection of witnesses, and victims. Yesterday, they asked for medicines and today, Ms. Pinter told me that the witness has ended up in the hospital. You can see from the summaries what kind of examination I anticipated for the witness. But if the second witness proves not to be able to testify, then I do not know. I mean, if he stays in the hospital, if his state of health deteriorates so badly that he will have to go back, then obviously he will have to be called again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you for your information. Could we have the next witness, please? Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Since we now since there is another witness in The Hague, is there any reason why the Prosecution should not be told who the witness is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Should we go into the private session, please very, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Mr. Krsnik, did you prepare a piece of paper? Examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, will you please look at this piece of paper and just nod and say yes, if that is your name. Do not pronounce your name aloud?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's not clear to me what the witness's pseudonym is as shown on this paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: NB.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because the documents we have been provided before has a different pseudonym on it. So this is not Witness I, which is what is indicated on the document that was just handed to our case manager this morning. Rather now this is Witness NB?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prior to the commencement of the Defence's case, we sat down and made a list of what the pseudonyms would be. We begin with NA, NB, NC, and all the way down. Why it's Witness I, I don't know, but NB is what I've prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: NB is the Witness I? That's the question I want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could be. You see, we -- the witnesses changed so perhaps this is why it happened. I really do not know because Mr. Meek did it and Mrs. Pinter and our distinguished registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me have a look at that piece of paper, please. Yes, you may continue, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness, and I wish to give you some instructions I always give to all the witnesses. Can you see the monitor in front of you? Since we speak the same language can you see a black dot moving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, because we are interpreting into English and French, you will see when the dot has stopped, it means that the text has ended and then you can begin your answer. Now, we shall stop so that you can see when it comes to it a stop. You've seen it. When it stops and then when it stops then you start your answer because our interpreters really have a difficult job. And also Their Honours have difficulty in getting full -- your full answers in the spirit of the language. Thank you very much for your cooperation. Now, I will start with my first question. Will you please be so kind as to introduce yourself briefly? Where were you born, what is your education and where did you work until 1990? And just slowly, always remember just go slowly, go easy, looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: I was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the municipality of Siroki Brijeg, the village of Uzarici, to be precise, is my birth place. I completed secondary vocational electrical engineering school, found a job with the Novo Gradnja construction company. After that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, we should have gone into private session because we are hearing now the personal particulars. So could we go into private session, please, and with all the apologies, because it is my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, but you have to get over this part of the testimony as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, would you be kind enough to tell us whether you participated in the war against the JNA or in the aggression by the JNA, how the units were established, how the Defence was organised, because as far as I could understand it, this is what you were working on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes. I participated in the war against the Yugoslav army and the reserves who attacked my place of birth and my town. However, that was much -- this -- the organisation of the aggression had been planned much earlier, which I knew, because upon the end of my military service, I expanded my military knowledge through the Territorial Defence commanding and staff exercises and drills. And in 1991 - I'm not quite sure when because this goes far back in history - I was invited by the then president of the municipality of Siroki Brijeg, who was at the same time the President of the war council, as it was usually referred to, to share my views with him, because it had been announced, or gossip could be heard that weapons could be withdrawn from the Territorial Defence of our municipality, the weapons that had been bought through the funds raised by the working people of that municipality and had partially been earmarked for the use of the businesses and companies there. On that day, when I visited him, we had already heard that during the night, the Yugoslav army penetrated our territory with vehicles and they entered the compounds of the tobacco factory where the weapons were stored. People were frightened because the aggression had already started on Croatia before. Knowing that I was familiar with the officers with whom I participated in the staff and command military drills and exercises, I decided to go to the tobacco station. The weapons had already been put on the vehicles, the troops had their helmets on, and they were commanded by an officer I had known very well, for whom -- I also know that he was later killed, Lieutenant Colonel Tomislav Pusara.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me allow you to lead you through the questions. The JNA, did they manage to withdraw the weapons from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: If you want a precise answer, the Territorial Defence was stripped of all the weapons. Only in one enterprise, eight rifles, M-48, 7.9 millimetre calibre, were left to the guards who were protecting that particular compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know whether this was done throughout the territory of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: At that moment in time, we prevented the weapons to go through the door, through the gate, and Dr. Zarko Santic, the then president, as far as I know, invited from the neighbouring municipality, and even the municipality of Imotski in the Republic of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness for my interruption. I think it would be helpful if we could at least get an approximate date in 1991, even the month, just so we have a better time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And Mr. Krsnik, I hope you get through this part as soon as possible, because according to summaries, this witness will mainly testify on the conflict in 1993. Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Precisely this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You heard the comments. Could you tell us approximately the date, the month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The date, I cannot really give you a precise answer because -- but I know that two months were very important. Whether it was February or April, I'm not quite sure, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Either February or April but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness corrects himself: 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Afterwards, the President of the municipality of Siroki Brijeg was changed. Andjelko Mikulic is the new president, and he invited me once again to come to a consultation meeting organised by the municipality. This was in April, 1991, because they had received 107 invitations for the conscripts who were supposed to be in the reserve units in the airport in Mostar. The invitations were sent out by the JNA. He asked me what I thought about it. Since at that time the Republic of Croatia had already been attacked, I thought that these people would be sent to the battle grounds, and I was absolutely against the war and I told him to halt the invitations, not to send them to these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let us go on. After April, in this war with the JNA, how did you organise the defence, how people are being weaponed, who issues the weapons? Very briefly, so this Chamber gets a picture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: In May, columns of tanks from the JNA were moving from the Northern Camp towards Siroki Brijeg and here, these tanks are stopped by the citizens of Siroki Brijeg, blocking the road with their passenger cars. People without any weapons are gathering in the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Whenever you use a date or a month, could you give us the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you please do it at every time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: In 1991, people with their bare hands are trying to stop the tanks, and then the politicians would come, of Bosnia and Herzegovina, headed by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, to this area, asking, demanding that the tanks be let through, which was also done. Afterwards, the five of us who were members of the council received indictments, accusations, and we were transferred to the court of martial in Sarajevo. In fact, we were supposed to be there and were tried and we got an eight-year imprisonment penalty by a Judge. This happened to me, Andjelko Mukulic, Jago Lasic, Mr. Ivica Martic, Mr. Ivan Lasic and Mr. Marinko Mikulic. We were all sentenced to this imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: This was the court martial of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And these people who were sentenced were who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The President of the municipality of the government, the President of the Defence Secretariat, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what were the charges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The charges were that we jeopardised the defence capabilities of the country by preventing the reserve troops from leaving the territory, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: At that time, was there any organised armed force in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: No, there was no other -- there were no armed forces. However, knowing that this was a very serious moment in time, and having been familiar with the attacks on the direction towards Ravno in the south of Bosnia-Herzegovina, where the JNA forces were moving to, in our municipality, and as far as I know, in other municipalities, Crisis Staffs are being established, and the territorial staffs are also being established covering parts of the territories of the municipality itself. And on the 21st of July, 1991, I was appointed head of the Blato territorial, that is regional defence. It covered the villages that neighboured the municipality of Mostar and the city of Krusevo. At that time, we set up troops without any weapons, comprising hunters, and we used hunting weapons, demanding from them that they cover the territories that were exposed to air attacks. I failed to tell you that in the course of the movements of the JNA tanks on the 7th of May and the 8th of May of 1991, carried out a helicopter air attack in the territory of Privalj, Duzice and Crnac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Where are these settlements located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Duzice, in the Siroki Brijeg-Split section. Privalj also along the same route, and Crnac is located north of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: These troops are being established within the framework of individual villages on the voluntary principle or on the basis of other principles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: On the voluntary principle. I can tell you about a peasant, Bozo Pinju who had five children but he sold his only cow in order to be able to purchase the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The name of the gentleman, of the peasant, was Tomislav Pinu. Did I pronounce it well enough, "Pinjuh"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Bozo Pinjuh.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Because the name was not in the transcript, so as to make the transcript collect. The name is Bozo Pinjuh? Did other villagers or local population members also buy their own weapons and did they basically organise the defence of their villages or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: They were not only buying weapons. They explicitly organised the defence of the territory concerned, defending on the territory concerned and the possibilities that they had to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let us proceed into the year 1992. Could you describe us the manner in which wider, larger military units were established, that is the HVO, when the HVO was established, et cetera? I will not put too many questions to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Sir, before answering this question directly, I must tell you that before the establishment of the HVO, Siroki Brijeg and Mostar defence was led by municipal staffs, with the units that were established in September, well they had had a unit, for example in Siroki Brijeg, we had a battalion which comprised of the most elite young men, and on the 21st of September, 1991, they headed towards the Galac mountains in the Humitza [phoen] Region, because the aggressor, the JNA and the reservists on the 19th occupied these territories, from Capljina to Medjugorje, Citluk, Visovi, and the cliffs above the Heliodrom, i.e., the village of Krusevo, and had thus cut off the Mostar-Citluk route in the Kobilovaca village, thus occupied Orlovac and Kozica, two major cliffs or mountains in this territory, and all that was still unoccupied were Galac and Planinica. Had this been done, Mostar would have been totally occupied and the clashes would continue westwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I understand you well, had the -- had Mount Galac also fallen; Mostar could not be defended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: No, nor a single additional hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. When is the HVO established, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: In parallel to the defence of this line by the troops that were members of the municipal staffs, the HVO was established on the 8th of April, 1992, as you will probably know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How was it established and what was your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: At that time, in the system of the HVO was an operations person in the municipal staff of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how was the military section of the HVO organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The military section was organised in battalions and platoons but village troops continued to cover the individual territories. These were a sort of guards, village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was this also based on voluntary participation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes. Siroki Brijeg had three battalions at that time and Mostar as far as I know had nine battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were there any ranks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How were the commanders selected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The commanders were made on the basis of an assessment that somebody knew more than the others or on the basis of an authority which a person had with the friends and their neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: How did they get their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Nobody wanted to say it at that time but every possible avenue was explored.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know how the weapons were procured and how training was organised by the Muslims? How did they operate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Since in Siroki Brijeg we didn't have many Muslim population, yet I know that a small number of Muslims did participate. I know this on the basis of one example. At the beginning of the month of April, I visited the staff and I can recall that a man arrived there, a young man from Mostar, for whom -- whom I knew because he was an athlete, a sportsman, a karate man. His name was Suad Cupina and he insisted that weapons be issued to him, if any were available in Siroki Brijeg. He was particularly referring to hand grenades, so that he could defend his own territory in Mostar, the territory of Luka in which the Southern Camp of the JNA was located, and where there were a lot of APCs and tanks. In the Siroki Brijeg staff, this was resisted because it was believed that they too will need the weapons. However, upon General Praljak's intervention, who was there and who said, "Give it to this young man. Thank God there is somebody who is willing to defend himself."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you tell us how were the Muslims organised? Now, let me first ask you, did you personally participate in the liberation of Mostar in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes. I participated personally in the liberation. My assignment was to lead the forces of a part of Siroki Brijeg and the sixth battalion of Krusevo, from Krusevo, another platoon was then can commandeered along the Mostar, Scopalija [phoen], Blazit [phoen] Which was done by the current general, Miljenko Lasic so he commandeered through them on these sections, on his left-hand side, there were the Convicts Battalion units, strike units. One of them was led by Mr. Franjo Zlomislic. And the second one along the toughest section was led by commander Mario Hrkac himself, Mario Hrkac, Cikota.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you and your brigade, that is you and your units, I don't know how you were organised, did you participate in the final ultimate liberation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The liberation of those territories took place on June 11, 1992, and the home guard units did not continue with the persecution but this was rather done by groups of these units that were set up in order to enable the attack on the enemy, on Orlovac, to allow our families to return to this territory because they were -- had been expelled to the Republic of Croatia throughout the territory. My family too was expelled there, which I learned on the third day when I was with the troops. Somebody from the local community told me that a lot of other people from the local community and my family were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Tell us how were the Muslims organised in the defence of Mostar, who led the defence of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The HVO was the one who led in the defence of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who was the HVO commander at the time, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The HVO commander, well it was municipal staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, but who was the commander of the municipal staff Siroki Brijeg, the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In Mostar. In Mostar, I mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: It wasn't in Mostar. It wasn't a Croat, it was a Muslim, Jasmin Jaganjac, and the chief was a Croat, Petar Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Were the Muslims organised in HVO units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: In Mostar, I do not know the exact number. Later on, I know how they were organised because later on, I learnt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And which was the area that you liberated then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: That day --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, I don't mean that day. We have to move on faster.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Right. As of the 11th of June, 1992, until the 26th of June, 1992, the aggressor had been repulsed to the Vitez slopes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know how many Muslim villages were liberated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes. All the villages in around Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what were HVO's losses to liberate -- when liberating those villages and that area, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you the exact number but if I take it, and may the dead forgive me, I will take the liberty to say that there were about 30 fatalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So Mostar is liberated, and where is your place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: And I get the order to go to the main staff of the HVO, to Mostar, because it had already been established in Mostar, and was headed by General Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you were appointed as what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: I was appointed head of the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how long did you keep that office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: I kept that office -- well, I cannot give you the exact date but I believe it was the 28th of July, until the 1st of October, when I received the order from the chief of defence at the time to form the 3rd Brigade of members of the 8th Battalion Blagaj, 7th Battalion Gnojnice and Dracevica, 9th Battalion, Rodoc and Zenica, parts of the 6th Battalion Krusevo, independent company Buna, the 4th Battalion from Mostar, Tihomir Misic and to set up a battalion made up of volunteers from Siroki Brijeg because by the decision of the president, the Siroki Brijeg Brigade was sometime in August, demobilised or placed on the reserve as the military would put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When did the demobilisation start?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: When the war with the Serbs ended, a month or a little more later, when the operation of the liberation or the repulsion of the Serb forces to Podvelezje to the Velez foot hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When we say demobilisation, it means whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The home guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what about the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: It concerned the home guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what about the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The volunteers could join units and the units would be made of them and this one from Siroki Brijeg was one such and it was part of the 3rd Brigade of the Mostar HVO and I was its commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know how many soldiers were released? I mean volunteers and home guards. And what month are we talking about, sorry, what month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact month but I think it was August.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And the year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The year was 1992. And I couldn't really be quite precise when it comes to other municipalities but I know that the reserve forces -- that forces were sent to reserve in Siroki Brijeg, in Posusje --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And if the witness could repeat the fourth place, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, the interpreter asked you to repeat the last name, the fourth place. Would you please do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: These places. You said Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: And Siroki Brijeg. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, I mean the name of the places.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: In Grude, Ljubuski, and Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Grude, Ljubuski, Posusje these are all names of towns in Herzegovina. Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And tell us what happened to volunteers who had come from abroad and used to work in Germany or in Croatia? Did they go back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you a full answer to that question. I do not think so. I do not think that all of them went back. Some may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you as the commander, are you familiar with the decision that those who, for instance, used to work in Germany or rather went back to work in Germany, and they did not go back to the military units, that they generously helped or paid generous monthly sums for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I was about to object. It seem to me that the witness already testified that he could not give a full answer on that. And my second objection -- so I don't know that he has knowledge about this issue. Secondly, I suggest that the question is a leading question, which is directing the witness to answer as suggested by counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik, rephrase your question. And I have to remind you that we have to get over this part as soon as possible. What we want to hear is what happened in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, of course. I see that I am going through 1992 very fast, but this humble servant of a lawyer believes that we cannot gloss over 1992 and reach 1993 because otherwise we will not be able to understand what happened in 1993 and how it happened, and now we are moving to those relations in Mostar, the relations with Muslims and so on and so forth. Because I must follow the indictment. The indictment sounds as if it fell out of the blue sky, Croats attacked, without any reason whatsoever, all those poor Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Please, let us move on. Now, a question: Do you have any idea how the HVO was funded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes. I know that our citizens who worked abroad did not spare even their last German mark to help their countrymen in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you become a commander of a brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes. I became a commander of the brigade, it was the 3rd Brigade. It began to be formed on the 9th of October and on the 26th I was given the official decision that I would be -- that I would be appointed the commander of the brigade, to form it, of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Please do it slower because nothing is on the transcript. Witness, will you please take care? This needs to be interpreted into English and French. Their Honours cannot follow you because the interpreters cannot follow you. They are doing a very hard job. Will you please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes, I will try to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But if you concentrate on the screen and that block spot.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But this also applies to the counsel. Please, it is better to keep silent for a while rather than not to have it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it took me a long time to get used to it. And I still make mistakes but will you please -- let us both try to complete this examination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What was your brigade's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of my brigade was in Podvelezje, Visovi or Podvelezje, above the village of Gnojnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: See, it is still not in the translation so let us move slowly. Where did you say on Velez? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Visovi or Polvelezje, in the village --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Tell us slowly, letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Above inhabited localities, Gnojnice, Dracevice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Letter by letter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: D-r-a-c-e-v-i-c-e. Blagaj. And above the village of Rotimlja. And that would be the end of the border, except if you want me to list geographic concepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. All we need is your area of responsibility. And where were you quartered as the brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: My brigade, or better said, the command of my brigade was quartered at the Heliodrom Camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You said Camp Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes, Heliodrom Camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What year were you quartered there, which month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: 1992, the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And there was a camp there, was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Then why do you say the Heliodrom Camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: My grandfather and my father called it the Heliodrom Camp. The Northern Camp. The Southern Camp. All -- they were all barracks built, as a rule, by Austria-Hungary, and because of the billeting of soldiers -- because soldiers were billeted there, they called them army camps so that it stuck among our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That barracks is called a camp? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who else was stationed at the Heliodrom, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Apart from my command, there were also accommodated there members of my brigade who had been expelled from their homesteads and had no where else to go. Then also the reconnaissance company of the Mostar operational zone Baja Kraljevic ATG for a while, and I think it was in January, but I'm not quite sure, Juka Prazina unit, the Caritas storage space, restaurant and a kitchen, which was served by my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let us explain what does it mean "served by my brigade"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Well, we provided the personnel to work in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And that kitchen cooked for everybody at the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NB
utterances.text: Yes, for everybody there and for people on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see it is time to adjourn, and this is a convenient place and we shall then resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning, we will sit in Courtroom II. We will resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I apologise. Could the witness be cautioned about not having contacts over the evening? I know it's normally your practice to do that when we break for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, Witness, we have to remind you that you are under oath -- the earphone, the earphone for the witness. Well, Witness, I have to remind you that you are under oath here in The Hague so during your stay in The Hague, do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.
